summary: This informational document captures requirements for session peering of voice, presence, instant messaging and other multimedia traffic. It links use cases to protocol solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: For two phone networks to connect their users, each side has to say where incoming calls should arrive and where outgoing calls should leave, and both sides have to be able to work out the same thing from the address the caller dialled. This memo lists what the protocols must make possible for that to happen.

subtitle: What protocols must do so that SIP service providers can exchange voice, video, presence and messaging with each other.

tldr.problem: Two SIP service providers that want to let their users call each other have to agree on where signalling enters and leaves each network, how a call is routed to the right place, and how the exchange is secured.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists seventeen numbered requirements covering the advertisement of border elements, the session establishment data used to route a call, presence and instant messaging, and the security properties of each exchange.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document: it does not mandate a protocol, but it states what any solution has to do so that peering works the same way across different operator networks.

today: RFC 6271 is an Informational document from June 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a list of requirements rather than a protocol, so it says what a solution has to do without saying how to do it.

sections.title: What Session Peering Is
sections.content:
Peering at the session level represents an agreement between parties to exchange multimedia traffic. The document assumes that the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is used to establish sessions between SIP Service Providers (SSPs). Service providers are referred to as peers, and they are typically represented by users, user groups, enterprises, real-time collaboration service communities, or other service providers offering voice or multimedia services using SIP.

Peering at the session layer can be achieved on a bilateral basis, where direct peering is established directly between two service providers, or on an indirect basis via a session intermediary, that is, a third-party provider that has a trust relationship with both. The document first describes general requirements, then analyses the use cases in the spirit of extracting the protocol requirements that must be met to accomplish them. These requirements are intended to be independent of the type of media exchanged, such as voice over IP, video telephony and instant messaging. Requirements specific to presence and instant messaging are defined separately.

It is not the goal of the document to mandate any particular use of IETF protocols other than SIP by service providers in order to establish session peering. Instead, it highlights what requirements should be met and what protocols might be used to define the solution space. The document concludes with a list of parameters for the definition of a session peering policy, provided in an informative appendix, which should be considered as an example of the information providers may have to discuss or agree on in order to exchange SIP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Session peering is just an agreement to pass calls between two networks, either directly or through a third network that both sides trust. The memo does not pick a protocol. It sets out what any set of protocols would have to achieve, so that two providers can build compatible solutions.

sections.title: What Is Covered and What Is Not
sections.content:
The primary focus is on the requirements applicable to the boundaries of Layer 5 SIP networks: SIP entities, signalling path border elements, and the associated protocol requirements for the look-up and location routing of the session establishment data. Requirements applicable to SIP user agents, or related to the provisioning of the session data, are considered out of scope.

Service providers have to reach an agreement on numerous points when establishing peering relationships, and the document highlights only certain aspects of such an agreement. It describes the requirements relevant to protocols in four areas: the declaration, advertisement and management of ingress and egress border elements for session signalling and media; the information exchange related to the Session Establishment Data; specific requirements for presence and instant messaging; and the security properties that may be desirable to secure session exchanges.

Numerous other considerations of peering arrangements are critical to a successful agreement but are out of scope. They include information about SIP protocol support, such as SIP extensions and field conventions; media, such as the type of media traffic to be exchanged, compatible media codecs and transport protocols, and mechanisms to ensure differentiated quality of service for media; Layer 3 IP connectivity between the signalling and data path border elements; and accounting and traffic capacity control, such as the maximum number of SIP sessions at each ingress point or the maximum number of concurrent instant messaging or voice sessions. The informative appendix lists parameters that may be considered when discussing the technical parameters of peering, with the purpose of capturing the parameters that are considered outside the scope of the protocol requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo covers four things: how each side says where its border elements are, how a call is routed to the right one, what presence and messaging need, and how the exchanges are secured. Everything else in a peering agreement, from codecs to billing to capacity limits, is acknowledged as important and left out.

sections.title: Declaring and Finding Border Elements
sections.content:
For border elements to be operationally manageable, maximum flexibility should be given for how they are declared or dynamically advertised. There is a need for a service provider to declare or dynamically advertise the SIP entities that will face the peer's network, and the data path border elements are typically signalled dynamically in the session description.

Requirement 1 is that protocol mechanisms MUST be provided to enable a provider to communicate the ingress signalling path border elements of its service domain. The border elements may be advertised statically or dynamically, and there is general agreement that RFC 3263 provides a solution for dynamically advertising ingress border elements in most cases of direct or indirect peering. Requirement 2 is that mechanisms MUST be provided to enable a provider to communicate its egress border elements. For capacity planning, traffic engineering and call admission control, a provider may be asked from where it will generate SIP calls, and the provider accepting the calls may wish to know from where they will originate. Requirement 3 is that mechanisms MUST be provided to allow a provider to communicate its data path border elements to its peers; some providers engaged in interconnects do exchange this information statically, and some do not.

Requirement 4 is that the mechanisms recommended for the declaration or advertisement of border element entities MUST allow for peer variability. Some providers expose the same border elements to all peers, while others advertise specific ones to particular peers, to meet objectives such as routing optimisation and optimisation of latency or throughput for the best combination. A simple solution is to advertise border elements using DNS and RFC 3263 by giving different DNS names to different peers, but this has practical limitations because the SIP URIs containing those DNS names may be propagated by users, for example in the form sip:user@domain, and it is impractical to ask users to implement different target URIs based on the provider's desire to receive signalling at different ingress elements. The solution described in RFC 3263 is therefore considered under-specified for this requirement. Techniques used elsewhere in the Internet, in particular in content distribution, make DNS responses vary based on the originator of the query, and anycast services may also be employed at lower layers than Layer 5.

Requirement 5 is that the mechanisms recommended for the Look-Up Function and the Location Routing Functions MUST be capable of returning both a target URI destination and a value providing the next SIP hops, so that the proxy in the originating network can select the appropriate egress border element to reach the target. Requirement 6 is that the mechanisms recommended for locating a peer's border element MUST be able to convey how a peer should initiate secure session establishment; the required use of SIP over TLS may be discovered via RFC 3263, and guidelines on the use of the SIPS URI scheme are documented in RFC 5630.
sections.plainLanguage: Each provider has to say where incoming calls should be delivered and where outgoing calls will come from, and it may want to say different things to different peers. The requirements insist that the mechanism allow that, and that finding a peer's border element also says how to start a secure session once you get there.

sections.title: Session Establishment Data and URI Reachability
sections.content:
The Session Establishment Data is the data used to route a call to the next hop associated with the called domain's ingress point. User identities used between peers can be represented in many different formats, so the session establishment data should rely on URIs, and SIP URIs should be preferred over tel URIs for peering of voice traffic. The use of DNS domain names and hostnames is recommended in SIP URIs, and they should be resolvable on the public Internet. As for the user part of the SIP URIs, the mechanisms for peering should not require a provider to be aware of which individual user identities are valid within its peer's domain.

Requirement 7 is that the protocols used for peering MUST accommodate different types of URIs, that URIs with the same domain part SHOULD share the same set of peering policies so the domain of the SIP URI may be used as the primary key to any information about its reachability, and that the host part of SIP URIs SHOULD contain a fully qualified domain name instead of a numeric IPv4 or IPv6 address. Requirement 8 is that the mechanisms for peering should not require a provider to be aware of which individual user identities are valid within its peer's domain. Both are generally well supported by IETF protocols. When telephone numbers are in tel URIs, SIP requests cannot be routed in accordance with the traditional DNS resolution procedures, so the solutions built for peering must not be limited to Public Switched Telephone Network identifiers such as Service Provider IDs or Trunk Group IDs. Although the session establishment data may be based on E.164-based SIP URIs for voice interconnects, a generic peering methodology should not rely on such numbers.

Requirement 9 is that the mechanisms for peering MUST allow a border element to locate its peer border element given a URI type and the target provider domain name. Based on a well-known URI type, such as sip, pres or im URIs, it must be possible to determine whether the provider domain servicing the URI allows session peering, and if it does, it should be possible to locate and retrieve the domain's policy and border element entities. An originating provider must be able to determine whether a SIP URI is open for direct interconnection without requiring a border element to initiate a SIP request. Since each call setup implies the execution of any proposed algorithm, establishing a session should incur minimal overhead and delay, and employ caching wherever possible to avoid extra protocol round trips.
sections.plainLanguage: The address a caller dials has to be enough to find the right entry point on the other side. That means the domain part of the address is what matters, not the individual user, and it has to be possible to look up the domain and get back both the policy and the address to send the call to.

sections.title: Presence and Instant Messaging Peering
sections.content:
Two providers create a peering relationship to enable their presence and instant messaging users to collaborate with users on the other provider's network. The requirements focus on inter-domain subscriptions to presence information, the exchange of messages and privacy settings, and the use of standard presence document formats across domains.

Requirement 10 is that the mechanisms for exchanging presence information SHOULD allow a user of one presence community to send a presence subscription request to presentities served by another provider via its local community, including subscriptions to a single presentity, a personal, public or ad hoc group list of presentities. Requirement 11 is that the mechanisms for instant messaging exchanges SHOULD allow a user of one community to communicate with users of the other community via their local community, using methods that include sending a one-time instant message, initiating a SIP session for transporting sessions of messages, and participating in n-way chats using chat rooms with users from the peer provider.

Requirement 12 covers privacy settings. In some presence communities, users define the list of watchers that receive presence notifications for a given presentity, and such privacy settings are typically not shared across providers, which causes multiple notifications to be sent for one presentity change. The mechanisms SHOULD allow the sharing of some user privacy settings so that users can convey the list of watchers that can receive notification of presence changes on a per-presentity basis. The sharing must be done with the express consent of the user whose settings are shared, and because the information is privacy-sensitive the protocols must follow the security recommendations for presence information. Requirement 13 is that it should be possible for a provider to associate a presence document with a list of watchers in the peer community, so that peer watchers can receive the notifications, which enables fewer notifications between the communities while avoiding the need to share presentity privacy information from one community to the other.

Requirement 14 is that the systems used to exchange presence documents SHOULD use standard PIDF documents and translate any non-standard value of a PIDF element to a standard one. Early deployments of SIP-based presence and instant messaging gateways were done in front of legacy proprietary systems using different naming schemes or values for the elements and properties defined in a Presence Information Data Format document. For example, the value Do Not Disturb in one presence service may be mapped to Busy in another system for the status element. Beyond this example of status values, it is important to ensure that the meaning of the presence information is preserved between providers.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence and messaging need their own rules: a user should be able to subscribe to a contact on the other network, chat with them, and be told when their status changes. The tricky part is privacy. If the two networks each keep their own list of who may see a status change, the user is notified twice, and sharing that list needs the user's consent.

sections.title: Security Properties for the Exchanges
sections.content:
The document describes the security properties that are desirable for the protocol exchanges in scope, covering three types of information flow: the acquisition of the session establishment data based on a destination target via the look-up and location routing functions, the SIP signalling between providers, and the associated media exchanges. It focuses on three security services: authentication, data confidentiality and data integrity. It does not specify the mandatory-to-implement mechanisms.

Requirement 15 is that the protocols used to query the look-up and location routing functions SHOULD support mutual authentication. The content of the response may depend on the identity of the requestor, and the requestor may want to verify the identity of the systems that provided the response, given the nature of the data returned. Authentication also protects the availability of those functions against attackers who would send bogus requests to make the lookup consume resources. Requirement 16 is that those protocols SHOULD provide support for data confidentiality and integrity, given that the session establishment data may contain user addresses, SIP URIs and the location of SIP entities at the boundaries of provider domains. ENUM, SIP and proprietary protocols are typically used today for accessing these functions, and even though providers may use lower-layer security mechanisms, candidate protocols should meet the requirements.

For the SIP signalling exchanges, which are out of scope of the document, the desirable properties are securing the transport of SIP messages between the peers' border elements, with authentication of SIP communications desirable especially where intermediaries are involved, and providing an Authentication Service to authenticate the identity of connected users based on the provider domains. The fundamental mechanisms for securing SIP between proxy servers apply to peering, including transport-layer security of SIP messages using TLS, the protocol mechanisms to verify the identity of the senders of SIP requests in an inter-domain context, and the mechanism for verifying the identity of the sender of SIP responses.

Media security is critical to guarantee end-to-end confidentiality between the end users' devices, independently of how many peers are present along the signalling path. Media carried over RTP can be secured using secure RTP, and a framework for establishing that security using Datagram TLS allows for end-to-end media security establishment. Media can also be carried in numerous other protocols, over TCP, and encrypted over TLS. Requirement 17 is that the protocols used to enable peering MUST NOT interfere with the exchanges of media security attributes in SDP: media attribute lines that are not understood by border elements MUST be ignored and passed along the signalling path untouched.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of exchange need protecting: the lookup that finds the far end, the signalling itself, and the media. The lookup in particular should be authenticated both ways and kept confidential, because it reveals where a user's boundary equipment is. For the media, the rule is that the network must not get in the way of the end-to-end encryption the two users set up between themselves.

viz.caption: WHAT THE DOCUMENT COVERS AND WHAT IT LEAVES OUT

cells: Declaring, advertising and managing ingress and egress border elements
Requirements on SIP user agents and on how session data is provisioned
The session establishment data, and how it is looked up and routed
SIP protocol support, extensions and field conventions
Requirements specific to presence and instant messaging
Media types, compatible codecs and transport protocols
Layer 3 connectivity between the signalling and data path border elements
A sample list of peering policy parameters in an appendix
Accounting and capacity control, such as the maximum number of sessions

viz.caption: WHAT THE BORDER ELEMENT REQUIREMENTS ASK FOR

items.title: Ingress border elements
items.text: A provider must be able to tell its peers where incoming session signalling should be delivered.

items.title: Egress border elements
items.text: A provider must be able to tell its peers where outgoing calls will come from, for capacity and admission control.

items.title: Data path border elements
items.text: A provider must be able to tell its peers where media will enter and leave.

items.title: Peer variability
items.text: The same mechanism must allow a provider to advertise different border elements to different peers.

items.title: Next hop with the address
items.text: The look-up function must return both the target address and the next SIP hop to use.

items.title: How to start securely
items.text: The mechanism for finding a peer's border element must also say how to begin a secure session.

viz.caption: THE THREE EXCHANGES THAT NEED SECURITY PROPERTIES

items.title: Looking up the far end
items.text: Mutual authentication, confidentiality and integrity, because the lookup reveals user addresses and the location of boundary equipment.

items.title: SIP signalling between peers
items.text: Securing the transport of SIP messages, with authentication desirable, especially where an intermediary is involved.

items.title: The media itself
items.text: End-to-end protection between the two users, with the network passing security attributes through untouched.
